hints.title: Check the logic before the algebra
hints.body: Line 1 uses the contrapositive. Negating “a divides b or a divides c” gives “a divides neither b nor c”, so the AND in line 1 is correct.
hints.recap: Negating an OR requires both alternatives to fail.
hints.pitfall: The false original claim does not mean its equivalent contrapositive was written incorrectly.
hints.pause: Check the remainder bounds stated in line 2.

recall.reminder: Reverse and negate both parts to form the contrapositive.

hints.title: Keep remainders within range
hints.body: When an expression is called a remainder on division by positive a, check 0≤r<a.
hints.recap: A multiple of a plus a leftover is not automatically division-algorithm form.
hints.pitfall: Two bounded remainders can have a product outside the remainder range.
hints.pause: Check each interpretation in the proof against the required range.

recall.reminder: A multiple of a plus a leftover is not automatically division-algorithm form.

hints.title: Test a composite divisor
hints.body: Choose a composite divisor that is a product of two smaller positive factors; try those factors as the nonzero remainders.
hints.recap: A numerical check can distinguish valid expansion from invalid interpretation.
hints.pitfall: Find the earliest unsupported line, not only a later false conclusion.
hints.pause: Calculate the product remainder and use it to inspect adjacent proof lines.

recall.reminder: A numerical check can distinguish valid expansion from invalid interpretation.

solution:
Lines 1–4 are valid. In line 5, rs is incorrectly declared to be the remainder: it need not satisfy 0≤rs<a. The actual remainder is what is left after any further multiples of a are removed from rs.

For a=6, b=2 and c=3, the product rs is 6 but the remainder is 0. Hence positivity in line 6 cannot rescue the argument. Line 5 is the error: answer E.
knowledgePattern: Locate the first invalid remainder claim in a contrapositive proof
